idiom_name: Selenium PageFactory: @FindBy/WebElement fields initialised by PageFactory.initElements
implementation_notes: The Selenium support library provides the classic Java realization: a class per page declares WebElement (or List<WebElement>) fields annotated with @FindBy/@FindBys and is created through PageFactory.initElements(driver, Page.class), which installs dynamic proxies so every field call re-resolves the element lazily; @CacheLookup opts a provably stable element into a single lookup, and the class's methods expose the page's services. What the factory cannot supply is the design: assertions stay in the tests, navigation methods return the next page object, and the driver reference stays private. Choose it for field-style pages with lazy re-resolution; choose the explicit-By variant when annotations feel too implicit.
pitfalls: PageFactory.initElements must run before any field is used, or the WebElement fields are null and the first call throws NullPointerException (the wiki states the assumption explicitly).
The fields are dynamic proxies, never concrete driver element classes; code that casts a WebElement field or relies on its identity breaks.

The default lookup strategy uses the field name as the id, then the name attribute, silently coupling code to markup naming; declare @FindBy explicitly and use @CacheLookup only for elements that cannot change during the page's lifetime.
WebDriver is not thread-safe: page objects shared across parallel JUnit/TestNG tests need ThreadGuard or one driver per thread.

variants.name: Selenium 4: explicit private final By locators and service methods (no reflection)
variants.idiom_name: private final By fields + driver.findElement + explicit waits
variants.implementation_notes: The style Selenium's own page-object documentation shows: the class keeps private final By locators and a WebDriver reference, and each method calls driver.findElement(locator) - or WebDriverWait for slow pages - before acting, so element lookup is explicit and no runtime reflection or proxy is involved. It composes naturally with Selenium 4 relative locators and with page component objects whose constructors take a WebElement root. Choose it when the team wants ordinary Java semantics and grep-able locators; choose PageFactory when field-style declarations are preferred.
pitfalls: findElement throws NoSuchElementException immediately: without an explicit WebDriverWait (or the framework's expected conditions) the page object fails on slow pages, while a wait hidden inside every method can double the suite's runtime.
Locator constants are shared across threads while the driver behind them is not, so one page instance cannot serve parallel tests.

variants.name: Selenide: page()/open() and lazy element proxies without PageFactory
variants.implementation_notes: Selenide replaces both PageFactory and most of the page-object plumbing: a page class calls $(By.name("q")).setValue(query).pressEnter() and returns page(GoogleResultsPage.class); open(url, Class) navigates and instantiates, and its auto-waiting element proxies mean no initElements call and no explicit waits. Selenide's documentation contrasts the two styles and recommends the concise one, while keeping the rule that page objects expose logic, not elements (fields stay private). Choose Selenide when the suite is Selenide-based; PageFactory remains the choice inside plain Selenium projects.
pitfalls: Selenide proxies bind to the WebDriver of the current thread: reusing a page object from another thread, or after the driver was closed, fails inside the proxy.
Because $ returns a lazy proxy, keeping it (or a value read from it) across a frame or window switch targets the wrong context; keep fields private and re-query inside methods.
